verdict.rationale: Both PRs make the same fix: a Map from normalized email to its first position, with new appends recorded so duplicates within one upload still merge. Both add the same first-duplicate test, and the behavior is identical. B is slightly more direct: it normalizes each incoming email once and writes the index explicitly. A routes this through a `remember` closure and the `result.push(contact) - 1` trick, and normalizes appended emails twice. A's report is somewhat stronger: it says the new test was run against the old code and that both versions produced identical output on the benchmark.
a_issues: `remember(contact.email, result.push(contact) - 1)` relies on push's return value and is less obvious than setting the index directly.
Appended contacts have their email normalized twice (once for the lookup, once inside `remember`).
b_issues: The report does not say that output was compared between the old and new versions on the benchmark data, only the timings.
The comment claims O(1) lookups without qualification; this is minor.

verdict.rationale: Both changes make the same correct fix: a Map from normalized email to first index, updated as new contacts are appended. Both keep the first-entry merge behavior when the stored book has duplicates, and both add the same edge-case test. A's loop is more direct: it normalizes the email once and assigns the new index explicitly. B adds a closure helper, normalizes incoming emails twice, and relies on the less obvious `result.push(contact) - 1` idiom. B's report is slightly stronger because it says the new test was run against the old code, but the simpler code tips it to A.
a_issues: Report does not say whether the new duplicate-email test was checked against the original implementation.
b_issues: Normalizes each new incoming email twice: once for the lookup and again inside `remember`.
`remember(contact.email, result.push(contact) - 1)` hides the index assignment in an idiom that is harder to read.
The `remember` closure is a small abstraction for logic used in only two places.
